Triggers.value: Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I have to be on guard all the time
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

issues.explanation: The trigger set mixes a socially evaluative trigger ('being seen') with nonspecific discomfort/detachment, while the threat items center on danger from sudden sounds, home intrusion, and interpersonal harm. For a combat trauma profile, 'being seen' is not impossible, but here it is poorly linked to the stated threat pattern and stands out as the one trigger not plausibly connected to the strong Triggers→Threat and Triggers→Negative Appraisals edges.

issues.item: Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: Within Threat, hypervigilance to loud sounds and watching others for danger fit a combat-related threat profile, but specifically monitoring for someone entering the home implies a domestic intrusion threat context that is not supported by the triggers, memory, or appraisals. It pulls the profile toward a different trauma context and weakens cross-node coherence.

vignette: Samuel, a 46-year-old park ranger, had always felt a profound connection to the vast landscapes he patrolled. However, that connection had fractured after his deployment in a combat zone, where the chaos of war transformed his once peaceful existence into a landscape of unrelenting anxiety. He had been home for several years now, but the echoes of helicopter blades still reverberated in his mind, bringing with them a tide of discomfort that he could not shake. Even the faintest sound of an aircraft overhead would trigger a sudden spike in his heart rate, leaving him feeling detached and unreal as if he were transported back to those moments of terror, far from the tranquil trails of the national park he now worked to protect. These triggers led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, igniting a primal instinct in Samuel that told him he was still in peril. Each of these triggers led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, sending Samuel's body into a state of panic even when he knew he was safe. Each trigger sent a wave of panic through Samuel, igniting a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event, as if his body was screaming that he was still in peril. These triggers led to an overwhelming sense of danger that felt as real as the original event, as each sound ignited a primal instinct in Samuel that told him he was still in peril, reinforcing the notion that he was never truly safe. These triggers led to an overwhelming sense of danger that felt as real as the original event, making Samuel’s body react with panic even when he was aware that he was safe. The sounds that once might have blended seamlessly into the background were now sources of constant threat for Samuel. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found that almost anything could tip into a warning, as the background hum of danger he carried everywhere turned ordinary cues into confirmations of his fears. He found himself on high alert, scanning his surroundings for any unexpected noises that could signal impending danger. Living at that pitch of alertness, he found the world had become dense with reminders he couldn't stop reading — even the rustling of leaves or the echo of distant voices felt like warnings, confirming the sense of threat that shadowed his days. This hyper-vigilance seeped into his interactions with others; he watched people closely, bracing himself for any signs of aggression or hostility, convinced that danger was always lurking just beneath the surface. The constant sense of threat became the most convincing proof that his life had changed beyond repair, solidifying his belief that he was incapable of feeling safe again. This persistent feeling of danger quietly confirmed his fears that he was not the kind of person who would ever regain a sense of normalcy or security. Feeling this afraid all the time, Samuel had eventually come to accept the conclusion his body kept offering: that he was not the kind of person who got to feel safe. This persistent feeling of danger quietly confirmed his fears that he was not the kind of person who would ever regain a sense of normalcy or security. The constant sense of threat made Samuel believe that he was fundamentally broken, as if he was incapable of feeling safe in a world that had turned against him. Each loud noise reinforced his belief that he was in a world fraught with peril, leading to a cycle of tension and watchfulness that seemed inescapable. This persistent sense of danger kept the memories of his trauma close, as if he had to keep reviewing them to stay one step ahead of whatever came next. As Samuel reflected on his experience, he came to believe that he had permanently changed for the worse. The threat that shadowed Samuel’s days quietly confirmed the thought he worked hardest to resist — that this was simply who he was now. This conviction that he was broken kept drawing him back to the traumatic memories, as if he needed to pinpoint exactly where he had lost himself in the chaos. The guilt of inaction haunted him; he replayed every decision he made in the heat of battle, convinced he could have done more to protect his comrades. Each time these memories surfaced, they brought with them a cascade of negative thoughts, leading him to internalize the belief that he was broken and forever marked by his failures. This guilt intertwined with his memories, making them feel more vivid and real than anything else in his life. The belief that he was to blame for the chaos kept drawing him back to those moments, as if he needed to pinpoint exactly where he had lost himself, reinforcing the clarity of his traumatic memories. This conviction that he was broken made the memories more vivid and easier to find — they sat there waiting, proof of his failures during a time when he felt he should have acted differently. He could almost smell the acrid smoke of explosions and hear the desperate cries of his fellow soldiers, sensations that left him feeling trapped in a past that refused to fade. Each recall of those traumatic moments seemed to reinforce his negative self-appraisals, feeding into the belief that he would never be the same again. Samuel's interactions with his environment became increasingly strained as a result of these memories. The vividness of his recollections made it difficult for him to engage in the present, as he often found himself lost in thought, gripped by images of conflict that felt more immediate than the peaceful serenity of the park. The underlying sense of threat made it impossible for him to let go of those memories; they surfaced without warning, vivid and unwelcome, as if his mind was compelled to relive the chaos to maintain a sense of vigilance. The memories, rather than fading, seemed to pile onto his psyche, each recollection reinforcing the notion that he was forever marked by his experiences. On nights when the threat felt highest, the memories surged to the forefront of his mind, vivid and unwelcome, as if his body compelled him to relive the chaos to remain vigilant against future dangers. He felt like a ghost, wandering through the park without truly being present, haunted by the fear that he would never be able to escape the shadows of his past. In his daily life, Samuel's heightened sense of threat began to bleed into his relationships, particularly with his wife. He found himself withdrawing from her, unable to share the burden of his fears or the guilt that gnawed at him. The laughter and lightness of their past seemed like a distant memory, replaced by an oppressive atmosphere where he felt the need to guard himself against any perceived threat, including her attempts to connect. Once he had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, even mundane occurrences like rustling leaves or distant voices became alarming signals, confirming his belief that he was surrounded by threats at every turn. His inability to be vulnerable only deepened his sense of isolation and reinforced his belief that he was fundamentally broken. Finally, it was the sound of a helicopter overhead during a family outing that prompted Samuel to seek help. He had felt an overwhelming wave of panic wash over him, sending him into a dissociative state as he struggled to remain grounded in the moment. This was the wake-up call he needed; he realized that he could not continue to live in such a state of fear and detachment. As he sat in the therapist's office, he felt a mixture of hope and dread, uncertain of what the road to recovery would entail. What frightened him most was the possibility of facing those haunting memories, yet he found himself hoping for a way to move forward, to reclaim the life he had lost amidst the chaos of war. The belief that he was permanently changed kept bringing him back to the moment it had happened, making those memories feel more vivid and accessible.
